extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, communications and marketing teams, startup founders and anyone who writes press releases for media coverage
extracted.subtask_description: Guide to composing a standard-format press release that attracts journalists and earns media coverage, covering structure, content, tone, and practical tips (including AI-assisted drafting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard press release format
rubrics_metrics.description: These are the elements of a standard press release: Headline, Subheader / Lead, Dateline, Body, Quote, Company info (boilerplate), Logo, Media contact information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stick with the expected format — "This is not the time to get experimental" — so journalists can quickly find what they need and see you as a seasoned PR pro. The format helps them determine whether to cover the announcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose your target audience & angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, choose your target audience and the angle that matters for them; the angle that will interest readers of a specialist publication differs from a local newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and target the right journalists and outlets. If you pitch the wrong journalists, even a well-written release won't get you anywhere. Use media databases to find relevant contacts and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline — attention-grabbing and essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline needs to communicate the essence of what follows at a glance; recipients will scan it in a fraction of a second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the main takeaway, be concise, avoid clickbait. Pro tip: don’t use all capital letters or exclamation points in your headline. Short, valuable, catchy and clear is best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subheader / Lead — expand headline with facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional but recommended; a de facto extension of your headline to pack extra information at the top and expand on what makes the announcement worth attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the five W's (what, who, when, where, why). Don’t tease with “read more” or mysterious copy — stick with facts and use this space to convey the most important information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Dateline communicates basic info like the date and location of the announcement; typically at the introduction of the main body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bold the dateline and separate it from the first sentence with a dash. The dateline always contains the name of the city in capitals (state optional). The dateline does not have to include the date. Update the dateline when the release changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body — provide the who-what-when-where-why clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The body covers the details of the announcement and should answer how it is relevant to the outlet's audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a strong opening sentence (often a paraphrase of the headline). Prioritize the newsworthy angle and top-level details that help journalists imagine a story. Keep language objective (not salesy). Keep the whole release to a single page — if you spill to a second page, cut fat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes add credibility or more details and can illustrate importance, uniqueness or impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes are optional but recommended. Ensure the information in quotes helps journalists create a more complete conception of the story. Use a high-profile, credible source when possible. Avoid salesy language in quotes and make quoted people sound authentic and real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company info (boilerplate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The last paragraph is a short, flattering description of the company — the press-release equivalent of an "About Us" section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it short, complimentary (position in industry, awards, etc.), and include a link to your website. Put persistent claims (e.g., "California’s leading supplier...") in the boilerplate rather than repeating them throughout the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logo usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Include your company's logo as part of any professional press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a full-color logo and keep it fairly small. Placement is flexible (top-middle or bottom-middle are common). The logo is for brand identity and should not dominate the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media contact information & call to action
rubrics_metrics.description: Include contact details for the media so journalists can easily follow up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly indicate who handles media inquiries and provide a phone number and an email address. A simple call to action like "Please direct all media inquiries to..." is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness — is it actually a story?
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserve press releases for timely and newsworthy announcements; ask whether people outside your organization will care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story isn’t new, interesting, or consequential to outsiders, reconsider issuing a release. Avoid being 'release happy' and sending releases without clear news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness & front-loading the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Get the facts out quickly and succinctly; include the most newsworthy information in the first few sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists have limited time; if you bury the news deep in the release, they may not read it. Avoid long, self-promotional or adjective-heavy copy that resembles a book chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of voice (especially in quotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes and quoted people should sound real and not use inflated or unnatural vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make quoted speakers sound authentic to their voice and role (e.g., avoid a young person using unnecessarily complex words). Inauthentic quotes can undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective tone — not advertising copy
rubrics_metrics.description: A press release should be written in the most objective way possible and not as an advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid salesy language or promotional claims presented as news. The goal is to ignite journalist interest in a story, not to sell a product directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length constraint — keep to one page
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t let the length of the body push the total length beyond a single page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you exceed one page, there is likely material to cut. Journalists prefer concise releases that communicate essentials quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key messaging: what, why, what's next
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting (including with AI), identify clear key messages: What is happening, Why it matters, and What's next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being specific with these messages helps generate a tight draft and gives journalists clear takeaways. For AI tools: enter type, target audience and key messages; answer follow-up questions; then customize and edit the draft carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use AI and templates as drafting tools, not final authority
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-powered tools can create drafts, suggest edits, and recommend contacts, but you still need to know press-release best practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customize and edit AI drafts for tone, accuracy and relevance. Prowly’s workflow: enter details, answer follow-ups, edit the draft, and review AI suggestions (it flags improvements based on internal criteria). Always verify facts and tailor to the journalist/audience.
